extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters, patent attorneys, and patent agents preparing and prosecuting patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting, amending and defending patent claims to satisfy support, unity, subject-matter, industrial applicability, prosecution and enforcement considerations across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support requirement for claims
rubrics_metrics.description: You must always provide adequate support in the description for your client’s claims. You cannot add wholly new material in response to an examiner’s objections and should anticipate any narrower elements you may later need to add to the claims by embedding support in the description at the outset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The admissible degree of generalization is judged by the examiner in light of the prior art and varies by technology field. A fair claim is neither so broad it goes beyond the invention nor so narrow as to deprive the applicant of a just reward. Applicants may cover obvious modifications, equivalents and uses if it is reasonable that the variants will have the properties or uses ascribed in the description. Examples: a process disclosed for one plant kind cannot validly be claimed for all plant seedlings without convincing evidence; claims for synthetic resin methods limited to thermoplastics if examples only show thermoplastics; omitting a disclosed additive from a broad composition claim can render the claim unsupported. Professional tip: embed support for foreseeable narrower claim elements in the description from the start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of generalization in claim drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: The admissible degree of generalization claimed may vary depending on the field of technologies and related prior art; claims that open up a whole new field may be more extensively generalized than those that improve a well-known field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners judge generalization case-by-case. Broader protection generally requires more extensive disclosure; narrow protection may suffice with a single embodiment. Unnecessarily extensive disclosure is not prohibited but increases cost and public disclosure. Ensure reasonable evidence that claimed variants have the ascribed properties or uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application must typically relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept (the unity requirement; 'restriction requirement' in the U.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: ensure fair fee structures and prevent filing a plethora of separate inventions for one fee. Lack of unity is not fatal: examiner may require election of claims and the applicant may file divisional applications for unelected claims (time and cost consequences). Examples and analysis mainly pertain to chemical inventions but extend across technical domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity between intermediate and final products (EPO criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity is present between intermediate and final products if (i) they have the same essential structural element and (ii) they are technically interrelated (final product manufactured directly from intermediate or separated by few intermediates bearing the same essential structural element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity may also be present when structures are unknown if sufficient evidence leads a person skilled in the art to conclude technical interrelation (e.g., shared essential element). Families of intermediates and final products must correspond reasonably; intermediates used in different processes are allowed provided they share the same essential structural element. Mere other applications or effects of intermediates do not prejudice unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity in Markush-type claims (chemical alternatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a single claim defines alternatives (a Markush group), unity exists if the alternatives are of a similar nature and can fairly be substituted for one another. Under the PCT for chemical alternatives: (A) all alternatives have a common property or activity, and (B) either (B.1) a common structure is present (significant structural element shared) or (B.2) alternatives belong to a recognized class of chemical compounds expected to behave the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'significant structural element' may be a single component or a combination of linked components and must be essential to the common property/activity. If at least one alternative is not novel, re-evaluate unity. Unity may be apparent a priori or only a posteriori when prior art shows lack of novelty/inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim point of view (consistent point of view)
rubrics_metrics.description: All limitations or elements set out in a single claim should have a consistent 'point of view' (e.g., all steps in a method claim must be performed by the same party).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent point of view is important for identifying parties that could directly infringe. If inventive components are spread across parties, a single claim lacking a consistent point of view may make proving infringement difficult. Draft claims to enable direct infringement (or anticipate evidence for indirect infringement) and to facilitate enforcement/licensing. Examples: combined battery/flashlight claim that mixes parties may leave no single entity directly infringing; better to draft separate flashlight, battery, and connector claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft claims to facilitate enforcement and licensing (all-element rule awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should be set out so that imitation of the protected subject matter will be considered an act of direct infringement; at least one claim should read on embodiments made, used and sold by the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct infringement is often prerequisite to asserting contributory or induced infringement; product claims are generally easier to detect/prove than process claims. If claims do not read on the client's embodiment, the drafter may have misunderstood the invention or the client’s practice may have changed. Consequences include inability to mark products as patented and difficulties collecting lost profits damages. Use multiple claims targeted at different parties/parts when appropriate (e.g., client/server splitting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing claims during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be narrowed by (i) adding new elements, (ii) adding a limitation to a previously recited element, and/or (iii) further defining how previously recited elements interoperate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adding a new element, it should further define an existing structure/functional element or be relational; the new element must be present in the description (impermissible to create new relationships not disclosed at filing). Consider alternative amendments and counsel the client about the impact on claim breadth and enforceability. Examples: adding a removable cap to a pencil claim; further defining a light's direction to narrow scope. More on amendments in Module IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show amendments clearly during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Most patent offices require the drafter to clearly show any changes made to amend a claim during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depending on local rules, amendments may be submitted with editorial indications: bracketed notes like '[Amended]', strike-through for deletions and underlining for additions. Use these conventions to make the nature of amendments explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from patentability (subject-matter exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most jurisdictions exclude certain subject matter from patent protection; lists and scope vary by country (e.g., judicial exceptions in the U.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims are rejected on exclusions, redrafting may sometimes obtain protection (substance preserved, form changed). Software-related inventions may require particular wording to avoid exclusions. Biotechnology inventions require special care: some discoveries or exploitations may be unprotectable for reasons of public order/morality. Stay up to date with national/regional law developments and advise clients accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of products for use in excluded methods (medical/biotech caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where methods of treating a human or animal body are excluded, new products for use in those methods (e.g., substances, compositions) or manufacture of prostheses/artificial limbs may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish surgical/therapeutic methods from manufacture steps or outside-the-body manufacturing. For example, taking an imprint of a footplate or molding for an artificial limb is not surgical and may be patentable. Conversely, methods requiring surgical steps (e.g., measuring for an endoprosthesis) may be excluded. Reformatting claims (e.g., as industrially applicable tests) can sometimes allow protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for industrial applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The description should indicate how the invention is capable of exploitation in industry where this is not self-evident; for sequences/partial gene sequences, the industrial application must be disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere nucleic acid sequence without indication of function is not patentable; if a sequence is used to produce a protein, specify which protein and its function. If a nucleotide sequence is not used to produce a protein, indicate a functional activity such as promoter activity. Recast claims if examiner finds lack of industrial applicability (e.g., device for dispensing fashion advice might be recast as an inventory device).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading on a patent claim ('all-elements rule')
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim to read on an accused product or process, every element of the claim must be present in the accused product or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure at least one claim reads on the client’s own embodiments. If claims don't read on the client's embodiment, drafter misunderstanding or client changes may be the cause. Consequences include inability to mark products as patented and potentially reduced damages (lost profits harder to collect). See Module IV, section 1.3 for all-elements rule details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction in the courts (interpretation principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts interpret claims by reading the claims and the description; if not clear, courts refer to the ordinary meaning to a person skilled in the art and may consult dictionaries, handbooks, treatises and expert testimony. In the U.S., courts begin with ordinary meaning then review description and prosecution history for special meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a patent creates a new term or a term is ambiguous, define it in the description (the description can act as a glossary). Be extremely careful about potential ambiguities in the application and in prosecution responses because intrinsic evidence and prosecution history may be used to construe terms. Aim for a self-contained application understandable without external context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents (scope beyond literal words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions provide protection beyond the literal scope of claim words via the doctrine of equivalents, which may treat substituted features as infringing if they are equivalent in the invention’s context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrine of equivalents varies by jurisdiction and can be unpredictable. Example: a screw might be found equivalent to a nail for holding two widgets. Professional tip: draft claims as though doctrines of equivalents do not exist—give terms their ordinary and customary meaning to a person skilled in the art to maximize certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding ambiguity; defining multiple-meaning terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Words used in claims often have multiple dictionary meanings; courts will prefer the customary meaning in the specific art when relevant. If multiple meanings are possible and only one is meant, define the meaning in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When construing claim terms, courts may examine intrinsic evidence (claims, description, drawings, prosecution file) to ascertain the meaning consistent with the drafter’s intent. Use definitions in the description, and be mindful that technical dictionaries and expert testimony may be consulted; avoid leaving terms ambiguous during prosecution.
